Two edges from degree 1 to degree 2 plus one between the degree-2 nodes give a path of four; four edges from degree 2 to degree 3 plus one between the degree-3 nodes give a diamond; and two joined degree-3 hubs with two leaves each give a double star." width="100%"} The joint degree matrix records, for each pair of degrees `k` and `l`, how many edges join a node of degree `k` to a node of degree `l`. It fixes the degree sequence (the number of degree-`k` nodes is the sum of `joint_degrees[k]`, divided by `k`) and also how degrees mix along edges, so it pins down the degree assortativity as well. The matrix is given as a dict of dicts, `joint_degrees[k][l]`, and must be symmetric. Diagonal entries `joint_degrees[k][k]` count each edge twice, once from each end, so they are even. This is the same layout that `degree_mixing_dict()` returns for an undirected graph, so a graph's own joint degrees can be fed back in to draw a random graph that matches them. Edges are placed degree class by degree class between random nodes of the right degrees; when a chosen node is already full, one of its edges is moved to another node of the same degree, which keeps the joint degrees intact (the algorithm of Gjoka, Tillman and Markopoulou). The process follows NetworkX's `joint_degree_graph()`. The number of nodes comes from the matrix, and the nodes are created degree class by degree class in increasing order of degree. Nodes of degree zero can't be described by the matrix, so none are created. In a directed graph every edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Joint degree graphs are useful for: - null models that keep both the degrees and the degree correlations of a network - testing whether a property such as clustering is explained by degree mixing alone - generating assortative or disassortative graphs with an exact joint degree matrix ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [joint_degrees]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dict of dicts of non-negative integers: `joint_degrees[k][l]` is the number of edges between nodes of degree `k` and nodes of degree `l`. Must be symmetric, the entries of each row `k` must sum to a multiple of `k`, and diagonal entries must be even. Missing entries count as zero. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same other arguments always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the graph differs on every call. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `joint_degrees=` is not symmetric, has a negative entry, a row whose sum isn't a multiple of its degree, an odd diagonal entry, or more edges between two degree classes than they can hold. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Take the joint degrees of one graph: ::: {#4da2c445 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec original = ec.Graph().add_powerlaw_cluster_graph(n=40, m=2, p=0.3, seed=5) joint = original.degree_mixing_dict() joint[2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {3: 8, 4: 7, 5: 4, 6: 4, 7: 3, 10: 3, 11: 1} ``` ::: ::: A graph drawn from them is a different graph with the same joint degrees, and so the same degree assortativity: ::: {#a58b7db0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_joint_degree_graph(joint, seed=5) ( graph.degree_mixing_dict() == joint, round(graph.degree_pearson_correlation_coefficient(), 4) == round(original.degree_pearson_correlation_coefficient(), 4), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, True) ``` ::: :::
